name: Computer-aided design and engineering
definition: Using computers to design and test machines, structures or circuits, including computers designing other computers.

first_pass.what: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad at MIT, generally recognized as the first computer-aided drafting program (running by 1961 in earlier form)

first_pass_note: GM DAC-1 / Hanratty (from 1961) not confirmed as a milestone.

name: Automated scientific discovery
definition: A computer that forms hypotheses, runs analyses or experiments and reaches new scientific results with little human direction.

first_pass.what: Robot Scientist Adam (Aberystwyth/Cambridge, Ross King) autonomously generated and experimentally tested hypotheses about yeast genes, confirmed by humans (Science, April 2009)

doubt: 2009 Robot Scientist Adam may be late (DENDRAL 1965 and later systems).

name: Computer network and remote terminals
definition: Computers linked by communication lines so that distant users and machines can share data and computing through terminals.

first_pass.what: First ARPANET message sent from UCLA (Charley Kline, Leonard Kleinrock's lab) to SRI; system crashed after 'lo'

first_pass_note: Practical use (SABRE 1960, CTSS time-sharing 1961) not verified by search.

name: Global public information network
definition: A worldwide network that lets ordinary people at home look up information, send messages and use services from any connected terminal.

first_pass.what: Tim Berners-Lee made the first World Wide Web site (info.cern.ch) publicly available from CERN; Web software placed in public domain 1993-04-30

first_pass_note: Mass adoption (mid-1990s) not verified by search, so omitted.

name: Electronic mail and messaging
definition: Sending written messages from one person to another through computers and networks instead of on paper.

first_pass.what: MIT's CTSS MAILBOX let users of the same time-sharing computer leave messages for each other
Ray Tomlinson (BBN) sent the first networked email over ARPANET, introducing user@host addressing

name: Computerized information retrieval
definition: A machine that stores very large collections of records or documents and finds the items matching a query in seconds.

first_pass.what: NLM's MEDLINE online service began interactive searching from remote terminals at medical libraries (55 cities by Feb 1972)

first_pass_note: Archie 1990 and Google 1998 seen in results; Dialog launch year unverified.

name: Question-answering computer
definition: A computer holding broad knowledge that answers arbitrary factual questions put to it in ordinary language.

first_pass.what: IBM Watson answered open-domain natural-language questions and beat Jeopardy! champions Rutter and Jennings

first_pass_note: BASEBALL (1961) and Siri (2011) not verified by search; Watson 2011 chosen.
doubt: 2011 Watson is late; earlier question-answering systems (BASEBALL 1961, LUNAR 1971) may fit.

name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.

first_pass.what: Sony released the Librie EBR-1000EP in Japan, the first consumer e-reader with an E Ink display.
Amazon launched the Kindle at $399; it reportedly sold out in about five and a half hours.

first_pass_note: No Wikidata QID seen in results. Tablet alias not separately dated.

name: Electronic paper and rewritable display surface
definition: A thin surface whose printed image can be changed electronically, like a sheet of paper that rewrites itself.

first_pass.what: Nick Sheridon at Xerox PARC built the Gyricon rotating-ball electronic paper (sources say 1974 or 1975; the prototype was a rigid clipboard-like display).
Sony's Librie in Japan was the first consumer product to use an E Ink electronic paper module.

first_pass_note: Gyricon date is 1974 or 1975 depending on source. E Ink itself was not a continuation of Gyricon.
doubt: Librie 2004 practical use may be late (earlier e-paper shelf labels/signs).

name: Three-dimensional holographic display
definition: A display that shows images, maps or people as volumetric three-dimensional pictures viewable from several sides.

first_pass.what: Actuality Systems' Perspecta, a swept-volume display showing a 3D image viewable from all sides, appeared around 2001. Earlier volumetric prototypes were not checked, and a true hologram display is not established.

first_pass_note: Only a volumetric display (not a true hologram) was found. Earlier volumetric prototypes were not searched and the date is low confidence.
doubt: 2001 swept-volume Perspecta is late; volumetric and holographic 3D displays existed decades earlier (e.g. 1940s-1960s volumetric prototypes, holograms from 1962).

name: Computer screen display
definition: A screen on which a computer shows text, graphics or data to its user, in place of printouts or dials.

first_pass.what: MIT's Whirlwind computer, operational in 1951, showed real-time text and graphics on a CRT console.

first_pass_note: No mass-adoption milestone sourced. CHM hedges 'may have been the first'.

name: Real-time computerized situation display
definition: A computer-driven screen or plotting board that shows the live positions of ships, aircraft or objects tracked by radar and sensors.

first_pass.what: The first SAGE Direction Center (McGuire AFB, NJ) went into regular operation; consoles showed radar-tracked aircraft from computer data. Some sources give 26 June 1958.

first_pass_note: Whirlwind and SAGE prototype displays predate 1958 and are not separately dated.

name: Touchscreen and gesture interface
definition: Controlling a machine by touching a screen or panel, or by hand gestures and gloves read by sensors.

first_pass.what: E.A. Johnson at the Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern, published a capacitive touch display for computers (air traffic control). Published Oct or Nov 1965.
Apple unveiled the multi-touch iPhone; it went on sale in June 2007, making touchscreens a routine consumer interface.

first_pass_note: Johnson's design saw little use until the 1990s. Data gloves and gesture control were not researched.

name: Optical character recognition
definition: A machine that reads printed or written characters optically and turns them into data, for example to sort mail.

first_pass.what: The US Post Office put a high-speed OCR mail sorter into service at Detroit (Siemens in Germany also reported a mail sorting system in Pforzheim on 1965-05-31).

first_pass_note: Reading-machine origins before 1965 were not searched. The Detroit detail is only from a weak source, so the Smithsonian page supports 1965 generally.

name: Computer hacking and sabotage
definition: Breaking into, tampering with or disabling computer systems and their data, and the defences against it.

first_pass.what: The Morris worm, released by Robert Tappan Morris, spread across the Internet and disabled many machines. Creeper (1971, BBN, ARPANET) was an earlier experimental self-replicating program.

first_pass_note: Mapping to the kinds is loose. Creeper (1971), Brain (1986) and Morris (1988) are all candidates.
